item.title: Pipeline Hazards
item.description: Pipelining overlaps different stages of several instructions. This raises an immediate question: what happens when the next instruction cannot advance? On a simple in-order pipeline, the answer may be a literal stall: hold one or more stages until the obstruction disappears, leaving an unused slot traditionally called a bubble. Modern out-of-order processors are less dramatic. They keep many decoded operations in flight, wait only where a dependency or resource requires it, and continue issuing unrelated work when possible.

item.title: The Cost of Branching
item.description: When a CPU encounters a conditional jump or any other type of branching, it doesn’t just sit idle until its condition is computed — instead, it starts speculatively executing the branch that seems more likely to be taken immediately. During execution, the CPU computes statistics about branches taken on each instruction, and after some time, they start to predict them by recognizing common patterns. For this reason, the true “cost” of a branch largely depends on how well it can be predicted by the CPU.

item.title: Instruction Tables
item.description: Interleaving the stages of execution is a general idea in digital electronics, and it is applied not only in the main CPU pipeline, but also on the level of separate instructions and memory. Most execution units have their own little pipelines and can take another instruction just one or two cycles after the previous one. In this context, it makes sense to use two different “costs” for instructions: Latency: how many cycles are needed to receive the results of an instruction.

item.title: Instruction Scheduling
item.description: Consider the following function: #include <cstdint> std::uint64_t f(std::uint64_t a, std::uint64_t b, std::uint64_t c, std::uint64_t d) { return (a + 1) * (b + 1) + (c + 1) * (d + 1); } Written as a sentence, it appears to request four additions, then one multiplication, then another multiplication, then a final addition. The data dependencies tell a different story. The two products are independent: either can be computed first, and on a suitable processor they can progress at the same time.

item.title: Throughput Computing
item.description: Optimizing for latency is usually quite different from optimizing for throughput: When optimizing data structure queries or small one-time or branchy algorithms, you need to look up the latencies of its instructions, mentally construct the execution graph of the computation, and then try to reorganize it so that the critical path is shorter. When optimizing hot loops and large-dataset algorithms, you need to look up the throughputs of their instructions, count how many times each one is used per iteration, determine which of them is the bottleneck, and then try to restructure the loop so that it is used less often.

item.title: Theoretical Performance Limits
item.description: After optimizing a loop for long enough, every remaining instruction starts to look suspicious. This is a good time to stop asking “what else can I change?” and ask a sharper question: “what physical resource could make this version faster?” A performance bound does not predict exactly how long a program will run. It proves that, under stated assumptions, it cannot run faster than some limit. Comparing several bounds often reveals which resource deserves attention and which proposed optimization cannot matter yet.
